extracted.intended_audience: Investigators applying for NIH/NIAID research grant funding (e.g., R01, R21, R03, program projects, cooperative agreements, career awards, institutional training grants, RFAs)
extracted.subtask_description: Official guidance describing who reviews NIH/NIAID grant applications, reviewer roles and responsibilities, how applications are assigned and discussed, scoring basics (including the overall impact score and regulatory review criteria), and special procedures (streamlining, NRFC, deferred, foreign applications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplified Peer Review Framework factors
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications due on or after January 25, 2025, NIH will use the Simplified Peer Review Framework that reorganizes the five regulatory criteria into three factors: Importance of the Research, Rigor and Feasibility, and Expertise and Resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The new Framework replaces the prior five-criterion structure for most research project grant applications; applicants and reviewers should align proposals and critiques to these three factors when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five regulatory review criteria (Significance, Investigators, Innovation, Approach, Environment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional regulatory criteria are Significance, Investigators, Innovation, Approach, and Environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although reorganized under the Simplified Peer Review Framework for many applications, these five criteria still represent the substantive dimensions reviewers consider; assigned reviewers typically provide preliminary scores for each review criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall impact score
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review results in a numerical value, called the overall impact score, indicating reviewers' judgment of the likelihood that the project will have a powerful impact on its area of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The overall impact score is the most important factor for funding decisions. Investigators should aim to maximize this score by addressing the review criteria and clearly conveying importance, rigor/feasibility, and expertise/resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-meeting reviewer critiques and preliminary scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigned reviewers read the application thoroughly, write a critique before the meeting, and assign preliminary scores for each review criterion and an overall impact score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These preliminary scores inform which applications are discussed and provide the basis for the primary reviewer's presentation; applicants should ensure clarity and completeness in the application to minimize misunderstanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: SRO assessment of completeness, compliance, and responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific Review Officers (SROs) do an initial check of applications to ensure the key parts are present and, for RFAs, that the application is responsive to the funding announcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parts are missing or the application is nonresponsive to an RFA, the SRO may take procedural actions (e.g., defer review); applicants should follow submission instructions and RFA requirements carefully to avoid procedural problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer assignment and minimum reviewer counts
rubrics_metrics.description: CSR assigns primary and secondary reviewers plus at least one reader to each application; NIAID SRP panels assign at least three reviewers to assess each application (sometimes more depending on scientific needs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special Emphasis Panels (SEPs) or ad hoc recruitment may be used when specialized expertise is required; applicants should anticipate multiple reviewers with differing levels of engagement (primary, secondary, reader).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vetting for conflicts of interest and appropriate expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH peer reviewers are fully vetted for potential conflicts of interest and appropriate expertise requirements; any reviewer with a conflict is not allowed to review and must leave the room during that application's discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers sign conflict of interest statements; applicants can expect that conflicted reviewers are excluded and that panels are formed to match expertise to the science proposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconscious bias education and mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers receive orientation and ongoing education, including materials on unconscious (implicit) bias and guidance for minimizing its influence on review decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIAID SRP provides standardized materials (e.g., Pre-Meeting Orientation slides) and documents for panel chairs; reviewers are asked to periodically self-evaluate for bias and to consciously mitigate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlining / Not discussed (noncompetitive) applications
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH uses streamlining so reviewers can focus on highly meritorious and fundable applications. Streamlined (not discussed) applications are those reviewers consider noncompetitive; these do not receive an overall impact score but do receive individual criteria critiques from assigned reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CSR generally does not review approximately the bottom half of applications unless a reviewer asks to discuss one; NIAID may choose not to discuss applications based on application volume and number of awards. Any unconflicted reviewer may 'rescue' an application for discussion. Streamlining decisions are not final until the meeting adjourns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not recommended for further consideration (NRFC)
rubrics_metrics.description: NRFC is used for applications that lack significant and substantial scientific merit or have serious hazards or ethical issues; such applications do not warrant review and are generally not eligible for funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal investigators for NRFC applications still receive individual criterion scores and critiques from assigned reviewers. Avoidable causes include serious methodological flaws, safety/ethical concerns, or lack of substantive merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deferred review
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific review group can postpone an application's review if the group cannot determine scientific merit because information is missing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The group may contact the applicant for missing information or request another review at a later date; applicants should ensure submissions are complete and responsive to avoid deferral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion process, roles, and conduct at the meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: At the meeting the chair facilitates discussion, the SRO ensures compliance with policy, and the primary reviewer presents and leads discussion; program officers may provide programmatic input if present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflicted reviewers leave before discussion of that application. The group explores differences of opinion; other reviewers ask questions and typically skim the application during the discussion. The meeting structure is designed to produce fair, policy-compliant deliberations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of applications randomized
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers discuss applications in a randomized order rather than by preliminary overall impact scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Randomization helps protect the integrity of the review process and avoids biases related to reviewing order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion length guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: For discussed applications, the group explores differences of opinion; discussion generally lasts 10 to 15 minutes for investigator-initiated R01, R21, or R03 applications and may last longer for other application types reviewed in SEPs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussions tend to end sooner if reviewers are in agreement. Applicants should present clearly and concisely because discussion time per application is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of review materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Review materials are confidential; reviewers are not allowed to divulge information outside the meeting, and at the end of the meeting NIH staff collect and destroy materials used in the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants and reviewers should treat review content as confidential; applicants should not expect public disclosure of reviewer deliberations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for two audiences / Most reviewers scan each application
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigned reviewers read applications carefully, but non-assigned (non-conflicted) panel members generally listen to discussion and may scan or skim the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should write and organize the Research Plan for two audiences: (1) the assigned reviewers who will read in depth and (2) the rest of the panel who will rely more on the presentation and a skim—clear organization, strong signposting, and concise summary points help both groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign application extra review considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualified foreign investigators have an extra review step to assess whether comparable work is being done in the United States; if comparable work exists in the U.S., the grant may not be funded. Reviewers also consider relevance to the NIAID mission and whether the research is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign institutions researching select agents must follow the NIAID Select Agent Research Review and Approval Procedure for Grants That Include Foreign Institutions. Demonstrate unique expertise or resources not available in the U.S. to strengthen the case for funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clustering and consideration of new investigators
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, CSR committees evaluate applications from new investigators together as a separate group to ensure at least half of them are reviewed and to help NIH meet funding targets for new investigators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New investigator status may affect review grouping (clustering) and programmatic decisions; applicants who are new investigators should be aware of these protections and how their application may be compared.

rubrics_metrics.name: SRO operational responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific Review Officers recruit reviewers, state policies at the meeting, create streamlined application lists, manage review logistics, and write summary statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SROs are NIH staff (often with Ph.D.s) who ensure the review follows policy and produce official documentation of critique and scores; understanding SRO roles helps applicants interpret summary statements and procedural outcomes.
